objectives: Hear /z/ at the beginning of familiar spoken words such as zip, zap, zig, zag, and zen.
Connect initial /z/ to uppercase Z and lowercase z.
Distinguish the voiced /z/ sound from the contrasting /s/ sound.
Identify the first phoneme before looking at the written letter.
concepts: Initial phonemes occur at the beginning of a spoken word.
Z and z commonly represent /z/ at the beginning of taught words.
The /z/ sound is voiced and can be felt as a gentle throat buzz.
Listening and letter recognition are related but distinct skills.

definitions.definition: A speech sound produced with vocal-fold vibration.
The smallest speech-sound unit that can distinguish words.
A letter or group of letters used to represent a speech sound.

workedExamples.solution: Hear /z/ first; the word begins with the voiced /z/ sound.
The initial sound changes from /z/ to /s/, even though the words sound similar.
Both written forms commonly represent /z/ in the taught initial position.

commonMistakes: Naming the letter instead of producing /z/.
Adding an extra vowel after the isolated consonant.
Listening to the final sound instead of the first sound.
keyTakeaways: Listen first, then say the sound.
Contrast zip with sip to sharpen discrimination.

basic.prompt: How does /z/ differ from /s/ in this contrast lesson?

application.prompt: Why listen before looking at a word card?
application.answer: To practise phonemic awareness instead of guessing from the spelling.

higherOrderThinking.prompt: What should be practised if a learner names Z but cannot hear /z/?
higherOrderThinking.answer: Oral sound recognition and voiced/unvoiced contrast before letter naming.

mixedReview.prompt: Identify the target sound, blend or segment the word, then explain how you checked the result.
mixedReview.answer: Use phoneme-level evidence and reread the word or sentence.

mistakeBasedRevision: Naming the letter instead of producing /z/.
Adding an extra vowel after the isolated consonant.
Listening to the final sound instead of the first sound.
weakTopicRevision: If new-consonant-z accuracy is below target, isolate the weak sound or reading step, model it, practise with guided examples, then reassess using fresh items.

activities.name: type
steps: Say /z/ gently and let the learner notice the throat buzz.
Say zip, sip, zap, and sap in mixed order.
Learner identifies the first sound before seeing the word card.

activities.name: type
steps: Show uppercase Z and lowercase z cards.
Mix the cards with previously taught consonants and repeat.

outcomes: Identify /z/ in at least 8 of 10 spoken initial-sound items.
Match Z/z to /z/ with at least 90% accuracy.
Distinguish /z/ from /s/ in a controlled contrast task.

questions.question: Which word begins with the same sound as zig?
Which uppercase letter represents the same sound as z?
Which word does NOT begin with /z/?
What is the first sound in zen?
Which statement describes /z/?
options: It is voiced and can create a gentle throat buzz
It is always the last sound in a word

questions.question: Which contrast helps a learner hear /z/ clearly?
What should the learner say when asked for the sound of z?
Which word starts with /z/ and ends with /p/?
Which activity directly checks initial /z/ listening?
options: Sorting spoken words by their first sound

questions.question: Why might a learner confuse /z/ and /s/?
options: They are similar sounds that differ in voicing
Both always occur at the end

questions.question: A learner knows the letter Z but cannot hear /z/ in zip. What comes next?
options: Practise oral /z/ listening and contrast with /s/

answerKeys.explanation: Zig and zag both begin with /z/.
Uppercase Z is the capital form.
Zip and zap both begin with /z/.
Zip and sip contrast /z/ and /s/ at the beginning.
The task asks for the isolated speech sound.
Spoken-word sorting directly measures initial-sound listening.
Voicing is the key contrast in this pair.
Oral phonemic recognition should be strengthened before moving on.
